svg.aria-label: Diagram: the three custom role permission support levels and what each does, the measured distribution across 14,036 permissions, the pattern in the unsupported list showing it is the IAM guardrails, the six launch stages of which only DISABLED has an effect, and the silent omission when cloning a predefined role
svg.title: Custom roles: three support levels, three failure modes, and an exclusion list with a theme
svg.text: 73 permissions out of 14,036 are off limits — and the pattern in that list is the point.
Measured 17 Sep 2026 from the support table: 13,536 SUPPORTED + 427 TESTING + 73 NOT_SUPPORTED.
SUPPORTED · 13,536
Fully supported in custom roles.
Works.
Also the default: an omitted
support level means supported.
TESTING · 427
Google is testing compatibility.
ACCEPTED — and you might see
unexpected behavior.
Not recommended for production.
NOT_SUPPORTED · 73
Not supported in custom roles.
REJECTED — the request fails.
Loud, immediate, unambiguous.
A good API.
So attention points the wrong way
The set that quietly misbehaves (427) is far larger than the set that refuses (73). Audit for TESTING, not for walls.
The exclusion list is the guardrails — and that is why #32 is survivable
iam.denypolicies.* · iam.principalaccessboundarypolicies.* · orgpolicy.policies.* · orgpolicy.customConstraints.*
privilegedaccessmanager.settings.update · resourcesettings.settings.update · dataplex.assets.read/write/ownData
#32: whoever can EDIT custom roles can add any permission, so a custom role grant is unlimited access.
But they cannot add the power to delete a deny policy, unbind a boundary, or change an org policy.
The escalation reaches everything inside the guardrails, and stops at the guardrails.
Six launch stages, one that acts
EAP · ALPHA · BETA · GA · DEPRECATED
Informational. Nothing enforces them.
DISABLED — switches the role off while
leaving it defined. Cheaper than deleting.
Two mechanical limits
Up to 3,000 permissions per role.
No wildcards — every permission listed in full,
so the list ages as services add permissions.
Over the ceiling? Split: Custom Admin (1 of 2).
The catch: three ways to meet the same restriction, only one of them audible
List a NOT_SUPPORTED permission yourself → the request fails. You find out at once.
Clone a predefined role that contains one → the custom role OMITS it. Created successfully.
You asked for a copy minus what you dropped, and got a copy minus some others too.
Include a TESTING permission → accepted; you find out when production misbehaves.
Same shape as the #33 version-1 read: an operation that cannot represent your request, succeeding with the
unrepresentable part removed. Two subsystems, one habit.
Defence: compare what you got against what you asked for — not whether the call succeeded.
